doctrine: The Kingdom of God, Already and Not Yet
summary: Inaugurated eschatology, the kingdom has come in Christ but is not yet consummated; the framework for the whole NT
readingInstruction: Read Mark 1:14-15, Luke 17:20-21, and 1 Corinthians 15:20-28. Today is a doctrinal pause on the kingdom of God as already here and not yet complete. Notice the tenses: the kingdom has come, and the kingdom will come.
settingTheScene: Jesus began his ministry by announcing that the kingdom of God was at hand. The Jews expected the kingdom to arrive all at once, with the Messiah defeating Israel’s enemies and raising the dead. Jesus said the kingdom had arrived, and yet he spoke of its future coming. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 15, describes the order of events. Theologians call this “inaugurated eschatology,” or the “already and not yet.”
observation: “Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God” (Mark 1:14).
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand” (Mark 1:15).
“The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed” (Luke 17:20).
“For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you” (Luke 17:21).
“But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).
“But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:23).
“For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).
“The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26).
doctrinalFocus: The kingdom of God is God’s rule and reign over his creation, and in the New Testament it is both present and future. It is present because the King has come. In Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection, the decisive victory over sin, Satan, and death has been won, and the Spirit has been poured out. The powers of the age to come have broken into this age. It is future because the kingdom has not yet come in its fullness. Sin and death still operate, believers still suffer, and Christ’s enemies have not yet been finally put under his feet. The church lives between the first coming and the second, in the overlap of the ages. Biblical scholars call this the “already and not yet.” This framework fits the way the covenants unfold: the promises made to Abraham and David are fulfilled in Christ and have begun to be realized, and they will be completed when he returns. Christians have differed on the details of the end, such as the nature of the millennium in Revelation 20, but all agree that Christ will return, the dead will be raised, and God will be all in all. Until then, the church is not merely waiting. It lives as a sign of the kingdom, proclaiming the King and walking in his ways.
interpretation:
Mark records the opening announcement of Jesus’ public ministry. “The time is fulfilled” means that the long wait, the centuries of promises, is over. “The kingdom of God is at hand” means it has drawn near, in the person of the King. The response is to repent and believe.

Luke 17 shows another side. The Pharisees ask when the kingdom of God will come, and Jesus says it is not coming with signs to be observed. It cannot be pointed to on a map. “The kingdom of God is in the midst of you,” because the King is standing there. The kingdom is first of all a person. His healings and exorcisms are the kingdom’s invasion of the world, and when he casts out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom has come upon them.

Yet the kingdom is not complete. In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul writes of the resurrection and says that Christ is the firstfruits. The firstfruits is the first part of the harvest, and it promises the rest. Christ has been raised, and those who belong to him will be raised at his coming. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and authority and power. “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” So there is a reign now, and a final victory yet to come. When all is subjected to him, the Son himself will be subject to the Father, “that God may be all in all.”

This has practical effects. Because the kingdom has come, we have forgiveness, the Spirit, and a new identity, and we can obey. Because it has not fully come, we still groan, suffer, and wait, and we do not expect heaven on earth in this age. We are neither triumphalists nor pessimists. We live with joyful patience, praying “Your kingdom come,” and working in hope because we know how the story ends.
connection: Daniel 2:44 and 7:13-14 promise an everlasting kingdom. Matthew 12:28 says that if Jesus casts out demons by the Spirit, the kingdom has come. Matthew 6:10 teaches us to pray for the kingdom to come. Romans 8:18-25 describes the groaning of creation as we wait. Hebrews 2:8 says we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. Ephesians 1:13-14 calls the Spirit a guarantee of our inheritance. Revelation 11:15 and 21:1-5 describe the final arrival.
application:
Pray “Your kingdom come” today, thinking of both the ways it has come and the ways it has not.

Where do you see signs of the kingdom in your church or neighborhood? Thank God for them.

When you are discouraged by the world, remember that Christ must reign until every enemy, including death, is under his feet.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that in Jesus the kingdom has come.
Thank him for the firstfruits of the resurrection.
Ask him to teach you to live between the already and the not yet.
